newsitem.title: USA: Muni underwriting spreads continue to shrink.
newsitem.headline: Muni underwriting spreads continue to shrink.

text.p: The overall underwriting spread earned by municipal bond dealers continued to decline in 1996, falling to $7.77 per bond from $7.96 per bond in 1995, according to Securities Data Co.

The trend of declining spreads continued its long fall started in the 1980s, when the gross underwriting spread per $1,000 bond was nearly $24 in 1981. Since then, a variety of factors have combined to chip away at the overall spread and profitability, spurring a number of large and small firms to get out of the municipal bond business.

The gross underwriting spread is the difference between the offering price to investors by an underwriter and the purchase price the underwriter pays the issuer, and can include underwriting fees, managers' fees, average takedowns and expenses.

The only glimmer of hope for underwriters seen in the spread statistics was the uptick in fees earned on competitive underwriting. The average gross spread for a competitive deal was $7.57 per $1,000 par value, up from $6.85 in 1995. The increase may be attributed in part to more bond deals being done through competitive sales -- $47 billion in 1996 vs. $41 billion in 1995 -- and more risk being built into the fees that underwriters charge for those issues.

However, fees earned on negotiated deals -- considered the more lucrative segment of the market and the bread and butter of deals many firms -- slipped to $7.81 per bond on average in 1996, down from $8.23 in 1995.

Nevertheless, market players say they hope underwriting spreads do not go much lower, but they all agree the halcyon days of the early 1980s are long gone and spreads are unlikely to ever reach those lofty heights again.
"It can't go much further (down), and ultimately it will go wider again, (but) not a lot," George Friedlander, a managing director and portfolio strategist at Smith Barney Inc, said.

Market players attribute the decline in underwriting spreads to a host of factors, including increased competition among firms and fee cutting, erratic swings in bond volume, the change in the nature of the buy-side, public issuers' concerns about the fees they pay bond firms, and the reduction of overall risk and expense in underwriting municipal securities.

Issuers, for example, are more likely to get judged on how much spread they pay underwriters, rather than how well they do on overall yield, Friedlander said. Conversely, a corporate issuer like IBM may sweeten the spread to ensure the lowest overall borrowing costs, Friedlander said.

"Public entities are under much more scrutiny, and one of the things they are under scrutiny for is how much they pay underwriters, so they may not be getting an optimal result in terms of yield, but they may be getting an optimal result politically," Friedlander said.
However, there is a price to be paid for lower fees. With fewer firms out there and cutthroat competition, public bond issuers may not always get the best deal.

Wisconsin's Capital Finance Director Frank Hoadley said he is not rejoicing about spreads' sharp decline. While $24 is too high, today's spreads are not particularly healthy for issuers either, he said.

"I don't think at these spreads that we are getting the kind of distribution or underwriting risk that is appropriate," Hoadley said. The finance director agreed with Friedlander that issuers are sometimes too concerned about spreads to the detriment of overall issuer fees.
"I think it's very difficult for most people who don't work with bonds a lot to understand the relationship between spread and all-in cost based on the yield to the issuer," Hoadley said.
The nature of the buyers of public debt has also changed over the years, becoming an ever more important factor in how underwriting fees are calculated.
An underwriter at a New York City firm, who wished to remain unnamed, said the "institutional nature of the buyside" has driven spreads lower.

In 1981, mutual funds were barely getting started, and bonds were sold in smaller blocks to a broader base of buyers. Now, more and more retail customers enter the market through a fund like a Franklin or Fidelity, he said.

"In the bond market 20 years ago in order to move $1 million bonds you had 20 salesmen each trying to move 50 bonds," the underwriter said. "Now, you can have one salesman call Franklin, and if it's the right price, boom, it's gone."
Smith Barney's Friedlander said he sees more industry downsizing ahead given the current spread picture.

"I think there will be more firms leaving," he said. "I think there will be some more downsizing in terms of the number of bodies, and I think that in order to get the spread back, I think you need to go through a period of volatility, some credit problems, and that's not on the horizon yet. This is going to take a while."

Robert Estrada, chairman and chief executive officer of Estrada Hinojosa & Co, said even though firms are making a profit on spreads at current levels, some are deciding that the profit is insufficient for them to stay in the business.
"And I think that's unfortunate," Estrada said. "Despite sometimes losing to competitors, I'm a big proponent of more competition, and the more firms doing it the better.
Keeping spreads at healthy levels is in the best interest of issuers, and ultimately taxpayers, he said.

"It's going to be a real disaster for issuers if it gets to the point that there's only two or three huge Wall Street firms doing all the municipal underwriting business because they are going to have the big club over the issuers," Estrada said.
-- U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1655
